I have ordered a complete siege of the Gaza Strip. There will be no electricity, no food, no fuel — everything is closed. We are fighting human animals and we are acting accordingly.

Yoav Gallant (Israeli Defense Minister, October 9, 2023)

What kind of society consciously and deliberately sacrifices its own youth for political gain and tactical advantage? Today the overwhelming majority of Palestinian Arabs nurture a blind hatred of Israel. They have created a cultural milieu of vengeance and violence, preparing their children to become sacrifices in a death cult. The death of Arab children on the front lines — exalted as shahids or martyrs — has become a cynical weapon in the arsenal of Arab leaders. They have learned that when their children are killed they attract worldwide sympathy, because the death of any child is a tragedy and is presented as such in the media, whatever the circumstances. The criminal leaders of Hamas, together with intimidated Palestinian parents in Gaza, exploit their children in armed conflict, in contradiction with the values of the rest of the civilized world and in flagrant violation of international law and decency. Palestinian Arab children are in danger every time Hamas fires a rocket at Israeli civilians — not only because many of those rockets are fired directly from civilian areas, but also because many of them fail to reach their target and end up killing and wounding their own people. Some parents and social organizations protest against the barbaric use of children as human shields, but these are unfortunately small voices in the wilderness. Protecting our children is a universal trait that unites humanity, but under Hamas rule this norm has been perverted and turned into its exact opposite.

Eli E. Hertz (2011)

The terrorists had massacred the women, the children, the dogs, the cats, the chickens, the livestock… everything that could breathe or make a noise, raise the alarm. Then everything was burned in some ten hamlets in these ancient tribal highlands of western Algeria. At the end they kidnapped a few young women for the harem of the caves and forests. They would be raped, impregnated and then killed. The massacre made more than 1,000 dead in one night (perhaps more because many were not registered with the civil authorities). And when I gave this figure on my return to Oran, people grimaced and did not know what to do with it. (…) At the time, the Algerian elites, whom one calls “left-wing,” were living cruelly through Islamist terror. They had an early lucidity about the manners of the Islamist monster, its methods and its ultimate goal. One knew, before all the others, the cost of the caliphate. Death taught the great lesson, precise and enlightened. That was our advance on the West, this lucidity. That is why when the horror of 7 October in Israel occurred, I was doubly shocked. Doubly trapped. Doubly scandalized. Doubly mute. And doubly angry, to the point of losing my words. (…) Being Palestinian exempted you from everything: from working, from inhabiting the world, from joining humanity, from thinking about one’s failures, from liberating one’s own country. This routine cry was the rallying cry of a hatred that I discovered little by little over time: Judeophobia. Hating the Jew exempted us from everything. The Jew incarnated this refused otherness, threatening to the uterine “Arab” universe. This culture of paranoia and of the universal conspiracy of the so-called “Arab” world; this hatred that finds in a “cause” the occasion to bleach its obscure essence. Worse still, “liberating Palestine” authorized a tortuous and unknown role-play for the West: to replay decolonization by projection, its sublimated epic and also its advantages for the ego. Thus, in this so-called Arab world, everything could wait as long as one had not liberated Palestine. (…) Concerning the Palestinian intifada, Mahmoud Darwish, the immense Palestinian poet, even said this: “In the end, the intifada harmed the Palestinian people. It became a profession.” And the pro-Palestinian sentiment harmed Palestine, it became another profession. (…) And the 8th, the 9th, the 10th? I discovered this incredible extent of Judeophobia among my own people. This hateful irrationality, this criminal or ignorant consciousness, used as a pretext the right to be indignant at the horrible death of the Palestinian in Gaza. It produced only a monstrous compassion disguised as solidarity. I discovered this ambient, cultural, rallying and parading Judeophobia. In truth, among my own people, often, the pro-Palestinian clothed the anti-Jew and the nothingness in oneself after the decolonizations. But there was worse to live and to reflect upon. For from the first weeks, an idea fixed my mind on its impasse: why, in the “Arab” countries touched by the horror of armed Islamists, did secular, left-wing, modernist, educated elites take the defense of the Islamist “monster” in Palestine in the name of the decolonial? How could survivors of the Algerian civil war today “understand” the monster and excuse it, and defend it in the name of a hysterized and sublimated ideal of decolonization pushed to the point of absurdity? How is it that those who know the most about the “monster of the caliphate” come to play the most ignorant and make themselves its advocates? (…) To perpetuate the narrative of imaginary decolonization, to continue to make war on an imaginary West, to take themselves for heroes and Che-Guevarize themselves, the elites among us resorted to the most detestable of ruses: dressing the Islamist monster of Hamas in the prestigious and outdated garment of the decolonial, on the back of the Palestinian who was dying between the Israeli army and the Hamas battalions. Thus, even if one knows what a monster is, he will become by this grace a monster “from home,” therefore one of ours, therefore our representative, therefore our armed wing. Hatred of the Jew goes so far that it can accommodate itself to an alliance with the worst of a recalculated “good.” Those same people who from Algiers ran toward Western capitals and airports to flee the “monster” of the Algerian Islamist in the 1990s, there they are applauding a carnage in the name of the “remake” and the illusion of the decolonial.

Kamel Daoud (Algerian writer, 2024)

Massacres are often “explained” by the media as the product of ancestral hatreds, of religion or of ethnicity. (…) Certainly it is not doubtful that religious or ethnic factors can play a role. But it is more a matter of an instrumentalization of these factors, by leaders and organizations, than of an “explanation” of the massacre by the religious or the ethnic. […] But… the rational approach to massacre does not take into account the effects of another phenomenon: that of the very dynamic of the conflict induced by these killings. […] The repeated practice of massacre tends to “deregulate” the men who commit them, which gives their conduct the dimension not only of barbarity but of madness. (…) Why these strange rituals performed on the corpses? (…) The accusation of impurity is a “universal accusation” against those one is going to massacre. The initial murder, by suddenly creating a strong crisis of anxiety in the population, will in return provoke a vengeful wave destined to purify society of the hostile elements who are designated as responsible for it. Physically eliminating all those perceived as the vectors of this threat becomes the surest means of hastening this process of reparative and pacifying purification. While being organized centrally by the State, the massacres would thus be “carried” by a social reaction of a cathartic nature.

Jacques Sémelin (2005)

author: jcdurbant

text:
How often have we heard the line about “The Children”. The slogans and banners calling Israelis “child killers”. The “schools”. The “hospitals”. And the West keeps falling for it every single time. 

The West looks at a dead child and stops. That is not a talking point. It is how this culture is built. A child’s death is the thing you are not supposed to use. It is the thing that is supposed to end the argument.

A lot of people on the other side of this fight do not share that reflex. They have a different one. A dead child is not the end of the argument. It is the argument. It is content. It is leverage. It is a sacrament. The camera arrives, the world flinches, and the people who put the child in the blast radius call that flinch a victory.

This is the part the West is in denial about and keeps refusing to learn, because learning it feels cruel. 

IT IS NOT CRUEL!!!

What IS cruel is raising a boy to believe the highest thing he can become is a corpse with a caption. What IS cruel is teaching a girl that her value is the photo of her body in the rubble. What IS cruel is calling that “resistance” and then demanding that people who actually bury their children as a tragedy treat it as the same event.

In one moral world, you have children so they will outlive you. You keep them from the fire. You lie over them if you have to. But in the other, fertility is inventory. “Offspring bombs.” Birth as a supply line. Martyrdom as a career path you assign before the kid can read. The child does not have to understand the cause. The child only has to be young enough for the picture to work.

That is why the propaganda about “the children” is so effective in London, New York, Toronto and Paris, and so incomplete. The Western audience is being shown the outcome and never the doctrine. They see the small shroud and they fill in their own meaning… that someone must have wanted that child alive, and someone else wanted him dead. 

Sometimes that is true. Often it is not the whole truth. Sometimes the people firing from the school, the people forbidding evacuation, the people dressing kindergarteners in toy suicide belts, wanted the child exactly where he was. Not because they are cartoon villains who hate their own sons. But because they have a theory of war in which their dead children are more useful than their living ones.

Listen to how they talk when they are not performing for English. Death is not the cost. Death is the product. “We love death more than you love life” is not poetry. It is a strategy memo. If you love life, you will hesitate. If they love the funeral more than the future, they will not. Your mercy becomes their ammunition. Your newsroom becomes their delivery system. You cannot look away from a dead child, and they know you cannot look away, so they will keep producing the one image you have no defense against.

None of this makes a child’s death less tragic. It makes it more tragic. The Western mistake is thinking tragedy is a shared language. It is not. For you, the small body is the thing you would give anything to prevent. For them, it is the thing they can spend. 

Until the West can hold both facts in its head at the same time, that the child is innocent, and that an ideology is trying to cash that innocence in, it will keep losing a war that is being fought in the one place it refuses to look. And that is the difference between grief and appetite.

text:
Mug and Beer
Two Slavic countries with a history.

We were having pizza. I was drinking beer when Mary handed me the mug. The mug is from Krakow; the beer is from Lviv. Our daughter brought me the mug from one of her trips to Krakow; her company has an office there. Because it’s a huge cup and a bit heavy, I only use it for special occasions. I prefer using a smaller glass so that I can’t get carried away.

As I poured beer into the mug and placed it beside the bottle, I was struck by the symbolism of the two objects. Two countries, sharing a border, one is fighting for its life against a ruthless enemy, the other is preparing to defend itself against the same enemy. There is quite a history of violence between Poland and Ukraine, but I will not get into that here. I will instead tell you about the positive personal experiences I’ve had with both countries.

If you read my Substack posts then you know something about me. In short, I was born in a Ukrainian village on the Polish side of the border. I spoke Ukrainian at home and Polish in school. I had both Ukrainian and Polish friends. I came to America in 1955. I was 11 years old then. In America I too had Ukrainian and Polish friends. In addition, I also had other American friends, they were of all shades and complexions.

There was a school in our village where we were often subjected to communist propaganda, especially of the anti-American type. When I thought about that later in America, I realized that the propaganda was forced on the school. As an example, 2 books I remember reading, one was Robinson Crusoe and the other was about Russia winning the war against Finland. Crusoe is about self-reliance; it’s one of the most important Western values. But the other book was Soviet propaganda. Russia invaded Finland and took some land but only after losing 6 times more soldiers than did Finland. I don’t think that fact was in the book. I’m sure that the Polish teachers, the people and even most of their government were not communist.

At that time Ukraine was considered a captive country and Poland a satellite country, both with communist style governments and taking their orders from the Soviets. Some things I witnessed and heard about tell me that Poles and Ukies worked closer together than most would think. Packages and mail with money from America arrived undisturbed. I remember us going to Sanok, a 10-mile walk, along river San, to exchange dollars for zloty. No, it wasn’t to a bank, but to see a friend Mother knew there. At one time Father shipped us a bicycle which Mother had to sell for food. Mail like that did not work in the Soviet Union proper. There all international mail was intercepted, screened and if they deemed necessary was censored and even destroyed. And I suspect no money would ever get through. Remember, “Twitter” was like the Soviet Postal System until Musk bought it and renamed it to X.

Another case of cooperation. My older brother almost did not make it to America. He was of military age, and the Polish Army wanted him. As I was told by my oldest sister, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw intervened on his behalf. Somehow, he was whisked away to West Germany and from there the US Air Force flew him to England.

In America I didn’t pay much attention to what was happening in Eastern Europe until Reagan became president. I was too busy working and being an American citizen. Reagan was the catalyst that took down the Evil Empire. I was very happy for them when both Poland and Ukraine declared independence from communism.

In 1994 Ukraine was coerced to sign the Budapest Memorandum. That was about America, England and Russia promising Ukraine security if it gave up its nuclear arsenal.  In 2014 Russia took over Crimea and part of western Ukraine. In 2022 Russia fully invaded Ukraine. Either of these hostile military actions by Russia should have triggered the other 2 signatories to come to the aid of Ukraine by forcing Russia to back down and to restore Ukraine’s borders. But they did not. Breaking the security agreement by America and England was the biggest betrayal of a country ever.

In 2017, our daughter offered to take us to Poland. That would have been my first trip there since leaving as a young boy. By then I was in my seventies, and I wanted to see my birthplace before I got too old. We landed in Krakow. A man, an expatriate from Canada, working for my daughter’s company drove us to pick up a rental. My house, 22-Hłomcza, was still standing. The village has been upgraded since I was there. It was wired, the roads were paved, villagers had TV’s and cars. The historic Ukrainian Church was still there and beautiful as ever. My house was also upgraded. No one lived there for years but I saw evidence of electric and gas service. The straw roof was replaced with asbestos tiles, and a TV antenna protruded from the roof. But the dirt floor remained and the outhouse was still broken. The attached barn and feed storage also needed repair.

We went sightseeing outside of Hłomcza. We toured the foothills of the Carpathian Mountains. We spent time in Sanok where we enjoyed dinner at an “upscale restaurant”, McDonalds. In Krakow we visited the fire breathing Wawel Dragon. We took a trip on the Vistula River. We poured beer from long glass flasks and ate pork knuckles.

Our time in Poland felt like a breath of fresh air. Maybe after eight years of suffocating under a DEI president made it seem so. I loved every part of being there, and I still miss it. Everywhere we went, we saw people who seemed happy and industrious. I can almost imagine Alexis de Tocqueville feeling something similar during his visit to America.

Today Polish and Ukrainian lives are intertwined in a most profound way. Estimated demographics help show the scale of the connection. Poland has about 38 million people. Ukraine had about 40 million before the war and roughly 35 million now. Of the estimated 5 million Ukrainian war refugees, about 2 million are in Poland, meaning nearly 1 in every 20 people in Poland is Ukrainian.

Ukrainian refugees in Poland are not freeloaders. Most of them are either working or running businesses. A Polish think tank reports that Ukrainians registered more than 123,000 businesses in Poland since 2022. Ukrainians increased Poland’s GDP by $25 billion. Such large presence of Ukrainians in Poland has led to resentment among some that Russia is actively exploiting. I will not get into that here.

Poland has been at the forefront of supplying military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine. And most of the aid from other European countries travel through Poland to reach Ukraine.

In 2024 Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, "I am not ashamed to use these big words: it is here, in Ukraine, that the world front between good and evil runs.”

Poland and Ukraine, although they share a violent history, both share their hatred for the new Evil Empire.

Ray/Roman Badiak

text:
Skid Row, a densely populated homeless encampment area in downtown Los Angeles, has been a recurring site for allegations of election-related fraud, primarily involving paid petition signature gathering for California ballot initiatives rather than widespread ballot-box stuffing. Petition circulators are typically paid per valid registered-voter signature, which creates a financial incentive to cut corners in an area where people may accept small cash payments, cigarettes, or other items.

In 2018, LAPD arrested multiple people on Skid Row for similar petition fraud, including setting up tables near missions and paying individuals to forge signatures from voter lists.

The most recent documented cases occurred in 2026. In May, Brenda Lee Brown Armstrong, a longtime paid petition circulator from Marina del Rey, pleaded guilty to one federal count of paying people (including Skid Row residents) $2–$3 to register to vote so they could then sign petitions. She sometimes supplied her former Los Angeles address for the registration forms. She was sentenced in August to 18 months of probation and 120 hours of community service.

On September 10, 2026, federal authorities arrested James Brass (47, of Victorville, also known as “Lord”), along with petition circulators Courtney Price (49, of Florida) and Jateisha Herron (33, of California). They face charges of conspiracy to commit identity fraud in furtherance of a state felony. Prosecutors allege that from February to August they used a voter database to obtain real registered voters’ names and addresses, then paid people on Skid Row to copy that information onto petitions and forge the signatures. Brass and Herron allegedly signed false declarations claiming they had witnessed the genuine signatures. Brass received about $41,600 from a petition management company. He pleaded not guilty and was released on $10,000 bond. Officials have not publicly named the specific initiatives involved.

These cases followed videos (including from James O’Keefe-related efforts) and resident interviews showing cash or cigarette payments for signatures, plus FBI interviews of Skid Row residents in June amid questions about high numbers of voter registrations tied to shelters such as the Midnight Mission. Some residents described being paid to sign petitions or registration forms; others interviewed by outlets like the Los Angeles Times said they had not been offered money to vote for specific candidates. Prosecutors have described the schemes as undermining public confidence in the initiative process that shapes California law. Defendants in the latest case remain presumed innocent pending trial.

text:
seen/heard >5 reactions to deepseek4 "data is all that matters" claim with "welp research is over"

but that is a terrible take 

during the old days (2016-21ish), if you were hillclimbing - in most cases you had a few knobs and levers for improving the model: (1) some architecture decisions, (2) some loss fn/learning signal differences, (3) some training algorithm differences.

you really had to be creative to turn intuition into inductive biases which meaningfully affected the outcome (or come up with posthoc explanations for why your human-guided neural architecture search worked)

now, the data is your lever for improving the model and the behavior. each token is a knob, and you can scale to thousands or even trillions. each reward function. if you want to influence the model behavior through inductive biases - there are levers everywhere for those with eyes to see

really data has always been the key lever for model improvement and progress in the field (eg imagenet did way more for vision than rcnn)

but it was a lever that was impossible to move (pay mturkers to annotate the right data) and took time money and energy

now, for the same cost - you can apply an army of agents and spend millions of tokens of compute to calculate the optimal reward signal for each token of training.

what is stopping you from improving performance except better research ideas and compute/time (which can be reduced with better research ideas)

the surface area for research has only increased, eg the architecture of a data factory is so much more interesting / offers more opportunities for research than a model architecture.

the age of research is only beginning

text:
$VLO $MPC $PSX $DK $FRO $INSW $LPG $BWET SAUDI EAST-WEST PIPELINE: IMPLICATIONS FOR REFINERS AND SHIPPING

EXECUTIVE ASSESSMENT

The specific claim that Saudi Arabia’s East-West crude oil pipeline has suffered catastrophic damage at 8 locations remains unconfirmed. Contemporaneous reporting establishes a serious deterioration in regional energy security, including attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and escalating threats to Red Sea shipping, but does not independently establish the precise pipeline damage described by The Hormuz Letter. The distinction is investment-critical: a precautionary shutdown, a repairable reduction in pumping capacity, and a prolonged loss of the corridor would produce materially different outcomes for physical supply, refining margins, tanker employment, and equity valuation. The appropriate analytical framework is therefore a conditional disruption assessment, not an assumption that the pipeline’s full capacity has disappeared. 

A sustained interruption would nevertheless be unusually consequential because the East-West pipeline is no longer merely an alternative to an otherwise functioning export system. It has become an important operating route during existing restrictions on Strait of Hormuz traffic. Aramco stated in May that the pipeline had reached its maximum capacity of 7.0 million barrels per day, while its August results emphasized the continuing importance of the pipeline, storage, and export terminals to maintaining supply. Damage to this infrastructure would therefore impair an already important contingency route rather than simply reduce unused redundancy. 

For the equities under consideration, the central distinction is between scarcity of crude oil, scarcity of refined products, and scarcity of transportation capacity. VLO, MPC, PSX, and DK benefit when their realized product prices increase faster than their delivered feedstock and operating costs, provided their refineries remain supplied and operational. FRO and INSW benefit when available cargoes require more vessel capacity or when effective vessel availability contracts; they do not necessarily benefit when oil production and exports disappear. LPG, the ticker for Dorian LPG, represents a separate propane and butane transportation exposure rather than a direct crude tanker exposure. Its investment response depends on changes in LPG production, export availability, trade distances, and delivered arbitrage economics.

The most important implication is that a severe pipeline outage could simultaneously support U.S. refining margins and weaken portions of the crude tanker market. Conversely, a restoration of Saudi export capacity could reduce crude prices while increasing tanker cargo availability. Treating these securities as interchangeable geopolitical hedges would obscure the underlying economic exposures.

EVIDENCE QUALITY AND THE LIMITS OF SATELLITE OBSERVATIONS

The claim combines several distinct propositions: a fire occurred, the fire was associated with the pipeline, multiple locations were damaged, the damage was catastrophic, and the resulting operational impact was substantial. Evidence supporting an earlier proposition does not automatically establish the later propositions. A credible thermal anomaly near an energy corridor can support the existence of an unusual heat source without establishing the affected equipment, the number of independent failures, or the volume of oil no longer reaching customers.

NASA’s FIRMS documentation is particularly relevant. VIIRS active-fire observations have a nominal resolution of 375 meters, while MODIS detections represent approximately 1-kilometer pixels. A detection identifies thermal activity within a pixel rather than providing an engineering assessment of the infrastructure underneath it. Industrial facilities and gas flares can also generate thermal detections. Multiple pixels, repeated observations, and different satellite overpasses therefore cannot be interpreted mechanically as separate pipeline ruptures. Establishing 8 damaged locations would require spatially distinct, time-normalized observations supported by infrastructure identification and corroborating evidence. 

Similarly, a smoke plume extending more than 100 kilometers would not establish that 100 kilometers of pipeline had been damaged. Plume length depends on atmospheric transport, the duration of combustion, and observation timing. Even a substantial localized fire can generate a long downwind plume. The operational significance would depend on what was burning and whether the affected equipment was essential to sustained throughput.

The investment-relevant evidence would be a documented reduction in pumping capacity, revised export nominations, canceled or deferred cargoes, changes in downstream storage, and credible restoration guidance. An official statement that a fire has been contained would not, by itself, establish that full throughput has resumed. Conversely, continuing tanker loadings immediately after an incident would not prove that the pipeline was unaffected, because terminal inventories could temporarily bridge an interruption.

THE CURRENT MARKET BASELINE MAKES THIS DIFFERENT FROM AN ISOLATED OUTAGE

The Energy Information Administration’s September 9 outlook, completed on September 3, already described a materially disrupted oil market. It estimated Middle Eastern crude production shut-ins of 6.7 million barrels per day in August, versus 5.0 million in July, and projected global inventory draws averaging 3.0 million barrels per day in Q3 and 1.7 million in Q4. It also reported that August exports from Yanbu were approximately 50 percent below July and that Saudi Arabia had increased shipments north through the Suez Canal, creating a longer route for Asian customers. These estimates predate the alleged September 10 pipeline incident and therefore represent an existing disruption baseline rather than evidence of the new claim. 

The Financial Times separately reported August Saudi crude production of approximately 6.2 million barrels per day and crude exports of approximately 3.1 million barrels per day. Those figures underscore why the pipeline’s 7.0 million-barrel-per-day maximum capacity cannot be equated with a new loss of 7.0 million barrels per day. Actual production, refinery intake, export throughput, and shipping availability were already constrained before the allegation. 

Market prices were also already reflecting substantial stress. Reuters reported September 10 settlements of $107.63 per barrel for Brent and $102.48 for WTI, increases of 6.34 percent and 6.69 percent, respectively. The report attributed the broader move to escalating shipping attacks and supply concerns. These settlements establish the prevailing risk environment, but do not establish that the pipeline allegation caused the price increase. Attribution would require a verified event timestamp and a corresponding market-response analysis. 

The implication is that the incremental investment question concerns deterioration from an already stressed equilibrium. Earnings benefits already being generated by elevated cracks, freight rates, and trade dislocation cannot be counted again as new value created by this allegation. Incremental value depends on additional margin expansion, a longer duration of exceptional conditions, or a higher probability that existing elevated earnings persist.

PHYSICAL SUPPLY LOSS, INVENTORY BUFFERS, AND RESTORATION

The pipeline’s maximum capacity includes crude supplied to Saudi west-coast refineries as well as crude exported directly. Reuters reported in May that approximately 2 million barrels per day could supply domestic refineries, leaving approximately 5 million barrels per day available for export at maximum operation. It also reported that the line was principally carrying Arab Light and some Arab Extra Light, with heavier grades already curtailed. The threatened flow should therefore not be modeled automatically as an equivalent loss of heavy sour crude or as 7 million barrels per day of current seaborne exports. 

The relevant physical calculation begins with actual pre-incident throughput, subtracts the post-incident sustainable rate, and then adjusts for replacement supply and alternative routing. Inventory withdrawals can sustain deliveries temporarily, but do not eliminate the underlying supply loss; they transfer the burden to inventories. Crude retained upstream of an interruption is not equivalent to usable inventory downstream of it. National inventory totals are therefore less informative than the amount, quality, and accessibility of stocks at the affected delivery points.

Illustrative scenarios demonstrate the importance of duration. An incremental delivery shortfall of 0.5 million barrels per day lasting 7 days requires 3.5 million barrels of replacement supply or inventory. A shortfall of 2.0 million barrels per day lasting 30 days requires 60 million barrels. A shortfall of 3.0 million barrels per day lasting 60 days requires 180 million barrels. These are scenario calculations, not estimates of the alleged incident. They show why a contained operational interruption and a prolonged corridor failure should not receive similar valuation treatment.

The number of damaged locations is not a linear multiplier of the supply loss. Several damaged sections along a common route do not create several independent losses of the route’s capacity. They can, however, complicate restoration and increase uncertainty. The duration would depend on the critical repair path, the availability of replacement equipment, the ability to conduct work safely, and the testing required before sustained commercial operation. Repairs to localized pipe sections can have a different timetable from damage involving pumping, electrical, or control equipment. Continued security threats can also delay commercial normalization after physical repairs have been completed.

The allocation of remaining flows would matter as much as the aggregate reduction. Protecting domestic refinery feed could shift more of the disruption into crude exports. Protecting crude exports could instead reduce refinery runs and refined-product availability. Both outcomes affect the international market, but through different price and shipping channels. The same barrel should not be counted as a lost crude export and again as the entire volume of products that would have been produced from it.

CRUDE PRICES AND REFINING MARGINS ARE DIFFERENT EXPOSURES

A crude supply interruption is not intrinsically bullish for refiners. The relevant earnings variable is the difference between the realized value of the refinery’s product slate and the delivered cost of its feedstocks, adjusted for operating expenses and other capture effects. A refinery can face higher crude prices and lower earnings if product prices fail to keep pace, if substitute grades become expensive, or if feedstock shortages reduce utilization.

The favorable case for U.S. refiners is that lost Saudi supply reduces refinery production elsewhere, while U.S. facilities retain reliable access to crude and can sell into a tightening global product market. The existing distillate balance makes this transmission especially important. The EIA’s September outlook forecast U.S. distillate inventories below 100 million barrels during September and below the 2021–2025 seasonal range for an extended period. It also forecast diesel crack spreads above $2 per gallon during August through November. That is equivalent to more than $84 per barrel of diesel, but it is not the margin earned on every barrel of refinery feedstock. Product yields, other product margins, feedstock quality, logistics, and operating costs remain essential. 

The grade effect is more complicated than a general increase in Brent. Replacement demand for the threatened Saudi grades could increase the prices of competing sour or intermediate-quality crudes. Complex refiners do not benefit automatically from higher oil prices if their usual feedstock discounts compress. Substituting light sweet crude for a different refinery feed slate can change yields and encounter processing constraints. The relevant question is the cost of producing the desired product slate, not whether an alternative barrel is nominally available.

Brent-WTI widening would be helpful only where a refinery’s delivered crude cost remains linked to the relatively cheaper benchmark and its product realization remains linked to international prices. Increased overseas demand for U.S. crude could also bid up Gulf Coast feedstocks, limiting that advantage. Canadian supply can provide diversification, but greater demand for replacement barrels could narrow Canadian discounts rather than widen them. Geography, pipeline access, quality, and procurement contracts determine the actual benefit.

The distinction between accounting earnings and cash generation also becomes more important during a price shock. As a simplified sensitivity, a $20-per-barrel increase applied to 10 million barrels of net funded inventory would require $200 million of additional working capital before offsets from payables, receivables, hedging, or financing structures. A refinery can therefore report stronger margins while experiencing a temporary cash drain. Higher inventory market values should not be treated as an automatic distributable windfall.

For scale, a $1-per-barrel improvement in captured margin across 3.0 million barrels per day over 90 days represents approximately $270 million of incremental pretax operating contribution, assuming constant throughput and no offsetting costs. The same calculation demonstrates why a prolonged margin benefit is much more valuable than a short-lived price spike.

VALERO: VLO

VLO offers a relatively concentrated refining exposure to the favorable scenario in which international product scarcity increases while feedstock remains available to its operating system. Its refining footprint spans the U.S., Canada, and the U.K., giving it exposure to several product markets rather than a purely domestic earnings stream. The current asset base must also reflect the closure of Benicia in April 2026; historical capacity figures that assume continued Benicia operations would overstate available refining exposure. 

The starting earnings level is already elevated. Valero reported approximately $4.4 billion of adjusted refining operating income in Q2 2026, with throughput averaging approximately 3.0 million barrels per day. At June 30, cash was $7.9 billion and debt was $9.1 billion, with an additional $2.2 billion of finance lease obligations. These figures indicate meaningful liquidity to absorb working-capital volatility, but also demonstrate that the company is not entering the alleged event from a depressed operating baseline. 

The positive incremental thesis is primarily a duration thesis. Sustained disruption to Saudi crude or product availability could keep international buyers competing for replacement fuels, extending strong margin conditions. The benefit would be greatest where Valero can maintain high utilization, preserve feedstock flexibility, and realize stronger distillate prices without a comparable increase in crude procurement costs. The unfavorable case is that substitute crude becomes sufficiently expensive to compress capture, or that operational constraints prevent the company from exploiting the product-price increase.

VLO’s renewable diesel and ethanol businesses require separate treatment rather than being included mechanically in a conventional refining sensitivity. Valero reported positive operating income in both businesses during Q2. Their incremental response would depend on their own feedstock costs, product realizations, and credit economics, not simply the price of crude oil. Higher diesel prices can support renewable diesel realizations, but do not guarantee a corresponding increase in renewable fuel margins. 

At the business-model level, VLO is a strong candidate for exposure to sustained product scarcity. At the valuation level, the relevant question is how much exceptional refining cash generation is already embedded in expectations. Applying a normal earnings multiple to an annualization of an extraordinary quarter would overstate the durable value of a temporary disruption.

MARATHON PETROLEUM: MPC

MPC offers a combination of substantial refining exposure, geographic diversity, and midstream earnings. Its 13-refinery system has approximately 3 million barrels per day of crude capacity. Large Gulf Coast assets provide access to export markets, while inland refineries give the system exposure to different feedstock and product pricing relationships. Its integrated logistics network also provides flexibility to move intermediate products and optimize processing across facilities. 

MPC’s Q3 guidance illustrates why a single crude-price assumption is inadequate. The company guided to approximately 2.820 million barrels per day of crude throughput and an overall feedstock mix of 40 percent sour crude. The guided sour share was 55 percent on the Gulf Coast, 25 percent in the Mid-Continent, and 50 percent on the West Coast. The Gulf Coast can benefit from stronger export realizations while simultaneously facing more expensive replacement sour crude. Inland operations can exhibit a different margin response. 

The operating baseline is already strong: MPC reported Q2 refining and marketing adjusted EBITDA of $6.655 billion at 94 percent utilization. Further earnings improvement is therefore more likely to depend on margin duration and capture than on a dramatic increase in utilization. The risk is that a market model adds a large incremental throughput benefit to facilities already operating near practical limits, or assumes that benchmark crack changes translate directly into realized margins. 

Balance-sheet analysis should distinguish MPC from consolidated MPLX obligations. At June 30, MPC excluding MPLX had approximately $6.737 billion of cash and $7.176 billion of debt, implying approximately $439 million of net debt on that reporting basis. The much larger consolidated debt figure reflects MPLX as well. A sum-of-the-parts valuation must remain internally consistent: valuing the MPLX equity interest separately requires corresponding treatment of its earnings, debt, and noncontrolling interests. 

The resulting exposure is broader than a pure refining trade. MPC can benefit from product scarcity while retaining a substantial logistics component. That diversification does not eliminate cyclicality, but it can make MPC a more balanced expression of a prolonged disruption than a smaller, geographically concentrated refiner. Relative performance against VLO would depend on regional margin capture, sour crude costs, operational reliability, and valuation rather than on the direction of Brent alone.

PHILLIPS 66: PSX

PSX has several relevant transmission channels: refining, natural gas liquids infrastructure and exports, chemicals, and renewable fuels. Its refining footprint includes Gulf Coast, inland, Atlantic Basin, and West Coast assets. This creates opportunities to benefit from regional shortages, but it also prevents a uniform assumption about feedstock exposure or product realization across the portfolio. 

The company was already realizing substantial benefits from the disrupted market. Reuters reported Q2 refining adjusted earnings of $3.09 billion and a realized refining margin of $24.08 per barrel. Companywide net income was $3.85 billion, and reported net debt declined to $16.5 billion. These results establish an elevated earnings and deleveraging baseline; a new pipeline interruption would need to improve the expected future trajectory rather than merely reproduce benefits already recorded. 

PSX’s NGL business provides an additional connection to the shipping analysis. Its midstream operations include gathering, processing, transportation, storage, fractionation, marketing, and LPG exports. Its Sweeny-related infrastructure and broader NGL network could benefit if international customers increasingly source propane and butane from the U.S. However, earnings capture would depend on available capacity, contracts, incremental throughput, and commercial margins. An international LPG price increase does not automatically accrue to the infrastructure owner. 

This creates an important interaction with Dorian LPG. Higher U.S. LPG export volumes can support both infrastructure utilization and VLGC employment. However, higher freight rates also consume part of the delivered arbitrage available to exporters and importers. An investment model that simultaneously assumes unconstrained export growth, expanding terminal margins, and sharply higher freight rates must test whether the delivered trade remains economic. The available commercial surplus cannot be allocated in full to every participant.

Chemicals adds a different cyclicality through PSX’s interest in Chevron Phillips Chemical and its exposure to petrochemical products. In a disruption scenario, relative feedstock advantages can improve for some chemical producers, but weaker industrial demand and constrained logistics can offset those advantages. PSX therefore should not be characterized as either a pure refining beneficiary or an entirely defensive diversified energy company. Its several businesses can react in different directions. 

Overall, PSX offers the broadest set of potential earnings channels among the named refiners, but also requires the most explicit segment modeling. The appropriate valuation framework separates refining windfalls, infrastructure cash flow, chemical-cycle exposure, and balance-sheet improvement rather than applying a uniform geopolitical premium.

DELEK US: DK

DK offers a more concentrated refining exposure through 4 refineries with approximately 302,000 barrels per day of combined capacity in Texas, Arkansas, and Louisiana. That concentration creates meaningful sensitivity to favorable regional margins, but also increases the significance of an outage at an individual facility. Domestic positioning reduces the direct relevance of Saudi crude delivery interruptions to some procurement decisions, without insulating delivered crude costs from global competition. 

The current operational setup is relevant. In August, management stated that Big Spring had performed well after its Q1 turnaround and that no additional turnarounds were planned for the remainder of 2026. Management also emphasized the company’s high distillate yield. In a scenario dominated by diesel scarcity rather than a general increase in crude prices, those characteristics could support disproportionate earnings sensitivity, provided the system remains reliable. 

Reported results require normalization. Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $638.7 million, but $490.1 million excluding the RVO adjustment. The $148.6 million difference should not be treated as recurring margin capture attributable to the current physical refining environment. This distinction matters when translating an exceptional quarter into an estimate of sustainable cash generation. 

The balance sheet also differs materially from a simple consolidated-debt interpretation. At June 30, consolidated net debt was approximately $2.561 billion. Excluding Delek Logistics, DK reported $614.9 million of cash and $817.0 million of debt, or approximately $202.1 million of net debt. A characterization of DK as an extremely leveraged standalone refiner based only on consolidated debt would therefore be misleading. DKL’s obligations remain economically relevant, but should be analyzed within a consistent sum-of-the-parts framework. 

For scale, a $1-per-barrel improvement in captured margin across 302,000 barrels per day for 90 days represents approximately $27.2 million before taxes and offsets, assuming full-capacity throughput. This is a sensitivity calculation rather than a forecast. It highlights why a modest sustained margin change can be important for a smaller refining platform.

DK is consequently a potentially higher-sensitivity expression of sustained distillate tightness, but not an automatically superior investment. The smaller operating base makes reliability, regional basis movements, and the treatment of logistics value especially important. A strong diesel environment can produce a substantial earnings response, while an individual refinery outage can materially reduce participation in that environment.

text:
Books that won't bore the hell out of me but help in our 203k.. real estate acquisition and legacy building journey.

GROK: 

Skip the textbooks. You want stories and playbooks that map onto buy broken, fix it, keep it, pass it on.Closest to a 203(k) brainThe Book on Estimating Rehab Costs — J. Scott. Not a novel. You will use it. Line-item thinking for write-ups so you don’t “squeeze” escrow and blow a draw.
The Book on Flipping Houses — J. Scott. Same author, faster read. Treat it as “how contractors get paid to be wrong about scope.”
How to Invest in Real Estate — BiggerPockets (Greene / Dorkin). Skim, don’t worship. Good map of BRRRR vs house-hack vs land.

Acquisition without putting you to sleepThe House Hacking Strategy — Craig Curelop. Duplex/fourplex live-in math. You’ll argue with it. That’s useful.
Long-Distance Real Estate Investing — David Greene. Even if you stay local: systems, not vibes.
What Every Real Estate Investor Needs to Know About Cash Flow… — Frank Gallinelli. Drier, but short chapters and the only “numbers” book worth finishing. Cap rate vs cash-on-cash vs what you actually pocket after you live in one unit.

Sweat equity / build the thingThe Lean Entrepreneur is the wrong genre. Instead: Building a StoryBrand only if you ever brand the contracting side. Better: The Construction MBA — Matt Stevens. Contractor who wants to stop being the cheapest bid.
Younger Next Year is not this. For land/ADU mindset: Strong Towns — Charles Marohn. Why small lots and incremental units beat “buy a finished fourplex.” Reads like an argument, not a lecture.

Legacy (keep it, don’t flip it all)The Psychology of Money — Morgan Housel. Not real estate. Still the one that stops you from blowing the first good year.
Die With Zero — Bill Perkins. Counterweight to “stack doors forever.”
Buy Then Build — Walker Deibel. If the contractor brain ever wants a business instead of another door.
The Simple Path to Wealth — J.L. Collins. Boring on purpose; use it so real estate isn’t your only plan.

California-flavored, not sermonsHCD ADU handbook is free and ugly. Read the unit-count pages only.
California Landlord’s Law Book when you actually have tenants. Not before.

Order if you only read threeJ. Scott rehab estimating  
Curelop house-hack  
Housel Psychology of Money

That’s the 203(k) + acquisition + “don’t die house-poor” set. Everything else is optional once you’re writing offers.

Operation Shelter Me Conducted in the Cities of Loma Linda, Grand Terrace & Unincorporated areas of San Bernardino

DATE/TIME: September 4, 2026, 6:00 a.m., - 4:00 p.m.,
 
INCIDENT: Outreach Operation
 
LOCATION: Cities of Loma Linda, Grand Terrace & Unincorporated areas of San Bernardino
 
SUMMARY: The Community Service & Reentry Division's Homeless Outreach Proactive Enforcement Team (H.O.P.E.) and Innovative Remote Onsite Assistance Delivery Teams (InnROADS), and the San Bernardino County Probation Department, conducted "Operation Shelter Me" in the unincorporated areas of San Bernardino and the cities of Loma Linda and Grand Terrace.  This operation aimed to connect staff with unhoused residents, offering them housing, medical, and mental health treatment services, while addressing community safety concerns.
 
On November 5, 2024, California voters passed Proposition 36, titled “The Homelessness, Drug Addiction and Theft Reduction Act.” The proposition took effect on December 18, 2024, and reforms multiple laws from Proposition 47, which have been responsible for increasing homelessness, drug addiction, and theft. Proposition 36 includes several new Penal and Health and Safety Code provisions that deputies can apply during arrests when appropriate. These latest charges can carry enhanced sentencing and prevent offenders from being cited and released before their court appearance. 
 
During this operation, deputies focused on individuals with significant mental illnesses to link them with restorative mental health pathways. The results of the operation are as follows, and where Proposition 36 is applied: 
 
• Approximately 61 individuals currently experiencing homelessness were contacted by deputies.
• 25 individuals accepted referral information to assistance programs
• 36 individuals refused referral information to assistance programs
• A total of 20 individuals were arrested during the operation, which included:
• 10 individuals arrested for their in-county misdemeanor warrants
• 5 individuals arrested for their in-county felony warrants
• 1 individual was arrested for an outstanding felony AB 109 violation 
• 1 individual was arrested for PC 3056 - Parole Violation, a felony in the state of California
• 2 individuals were arrested for HS 11377(a) - Possession of a controlled substance, a misdemeanor in the State of California 
• 1 individual was arrested for HS 11364- Possession of drug paraphernalia, a misdemeanor in the State of California
 
The H.O.P.E. Team and other aligned resources will continue similar operations throughout the County over the next year, thanks to special "Community Concerns" funding, approved by the County Board of Supervisors. This funding allows the Sheriff's Department to address topics of concern, such as homelessness, mental illness, and community safety for county residents.
 
All subjects arrested during the operation are contacted in the County jail by the Sheriff's Transitional Assistance Reentry Team (S.T.A.R.T.) and are offered additional resources and reentry services.
 
If you know of individuals experiencing homelessness who need services, please contact the H.O.P.E. Team at (909) 387-0623 or hope@sbcsd.org.
 
Refer: The H.O.P.E. Team 
 
Station: Community Service & Reentry Division
 
Phone No. (909) 387-0623
 
Case No. N/A
 
SHANNON D. DICUS, Sheriff-Coroner
San Bernardino County Sheriff-Coroner Department

text:
Banks, Beaches, and Rapid Growth — Editorial Analysis

This essay offers a compelling political-economy narrative, illuminating how institutional quality, entrepreneurial freedom, human capital and social transformation can convert peripheral regions into engines of inclusive prosperity.

Introduction

The article uses Coastal Karnataka—especially Dakshina Kannada and Udupi—as a development model, showing how regions with limited natural-resource advantages can achieve remarkable prosperity through institutions, enterprise and human capital.

Core Argument

Karnataka’s development is highly uneven. Bengaluru became a global technology hub, while Coastal Karnataka developed through a different pathway based on:

Private enterprise and entrepreneurship

Strong banking institutions

Quality education and healthcare

Skilled human capital and migration

Tourism and services

Women’s economic participation

The region became a banking hub with institutions such as Canara Bank and Corporation Bank, demonstrating how financial inclusion can stimulate local enterprise.

Institutional Dimension

The key lesson is that government need not control every aspect of development. Its crucial role is to create an enabling ecosystem—good infrastructure, education, healthcare, connectivity, predictable regulation and space for private initiative.

Social Transformation

Women’s employment through the beedi industry, household enterprises and flower cultivation contributed to income diversification, empowerment and demographic transformation.

Challenges

Regional disparity within Karnataka.

Over-concentration of growth in Bengaluru.

Need for better connectivity and infrastructure.

Risk of coastal ecological degradation through tourism and urbanisation.

Way Forward

Karnataka should promote polycentric development, strengthen secondary cities, encourage MSMEs, invest in human capital, improve digital/physical connectivity and combine tourism with environmental sustainability.

Conclusion

Coastal Karnataka demonstrates that development is fundamentally institutional. Creating space for enterprise, knowledge and social participation can transform even resource-constrained regions into sustainable growth centres.

Keywords: Institutional Quality | Human Capital | Entrepreneurship | Financial Inclusion | Regional Development | Women’s Empowerment | Polycentric Growth

67. USO/BZ=F: Brent surged more than 6% to settle at $107.63 and WTI settled at $102.48 as tanker attacks and Strait of Hormuz disruptions intensified.

68. XLE: Energy outperformed while nine of 11 S&P 500 sectors fell, reflecting a classic supply-shock rotation.

69. AAPL: Apple rose 3.6%, one of the clearest mega-cap relative-strength signals of the session.

70. NVDA: Nvidia fell about 2.3% as higher yields and risk-off positioning outweighed AI-demand optimism.

71. MU: Micron fell about 4.7% as the semiconductor complex sold off despite ongoing memory-pricing strength.

72. BKR: Baker Hughes fell about 7% after its Chart-inclusive guidance implied lower EBITDA contribution than some investors expected.

73. COO: CooperCompanies fell roughly 15% after softer guidance and the decision to retain CooperSurgical.

74. AEO: American Eagle fell roughly 14% as investors focused on comparable-sales quality and tariff-refund support.

75. AVAV: AeroVironment gained about 4.5% after a strong quarterly report and record backlog reinforced defense-drone demand.

76. CMCSA: Comcast rebounded about 1% after the prior day's broadband-driven selloff.

77. CHTR: Charter gained roughly 4% as cable stocks partially recovered from the previous session's subscriber-loss shock.

78. GOLD: Gold fell more than 1% as higher Treasury yields and stronger Fed-hike expectations outweighed geopolitical demand.

79. ECB: The ECB raised its deposit rate 25 bps to 2.5%, its second hike of 2026, as energy-driven inflation pressures spread globally.

80. SPX TARGETS: Barclays recently raised its 2026 year-end S&P 500 target to 7,950 and its 2026 EPS forecast to $365, underscoring the tension between earnings optimism and rising discount rates.

👉 STOCKS TO WATCH

81. CPI: Friday's August CPI release is the next major macro catalyst and will directly test the market's roughly 70% probability of a September Fed hike. The BLS release is scheduled for 8:30 a.m. ET September 11.

82. ORCL: Oracle's post-close results put Friday focus on whether investors accept roughly $70B of planned fiscal-year capex in exchange for very high cloud growth.

83. ADBE: Adobe's post-close reaction will test whether 150%+ AI-first ARR growth is enough to overcome structural fears about generative-AI disruption.

84. CPRT: Copart's fiscal fourth-quarter results are in focus, with salvage volumes and pricing the key operating variables.

85. KR: Kroger reports Friday, providing a fresh read on food inflation, traffic and consumer trade-down behavior.

86. META: Meta remains a key momentum watch after the JPMorgan upgrade and Muse's rapid App Store traction.

87. AAPL: Apple will be watched for follow-through after Thursday's 3.6% gain and its premium hardware launch.

88. NVDA/MU: Chip leaders will be a key test of whether a hotter CPI extends the rate-driven rotation away from long-duration AI winners.

89. XLE: Energy remains the key hedge against a persistent oil shock, but sustained $100+ crude would increase demand-destruction and policy risks.

90. TLT/IEF: Treasury yields are the main cross-asset variable into CPI; another move higher could pressure growth, housing and small caps.

91. COO: CooperCompanies will be watched for stabilization after its outlook-driven selloff and decision to keep CooperSurgical.

92. BHVN/XENE: Biohaven and Xenon will be watched for further competitive repricing after the FDA partial hold on opakalim.

👉 DEEP ANALYSIS / MARKET INTELLIGENCE

93. ORACLE AI CAPITAL CYCLE: Oracle's RPO reached $664B while Q1 revenue was $19.3B — a backlog more than 34 times one quarter of revenue. The opportunity is extraordinary, but capex is now running at a scale that makes financing and utilization just as important as bookings. This suggests Oracle is increasingly an AI infrastructure operator with software margins layered on top.

94. ORACLE FCF / FINANCING: Oracle spent roughly $28.5B-$28.6B on quarterly capex and generated deeply negative free cash flow while completing a $20B ATM equity sale. The key read-through is that customer prepayments and equity financing are becoming part of the AI data-center business model. Growth can remain spectacular while per-share economics depend heavily on how much outside capital is required to build capacity.

95. ADOBE AI MONETIZATION: Adobe's AI-first ARR grew more than 150% while total ARR reached $27.5B. That is bullish but also sets a higher bar: AI adoption must eventually lift pricing, retention or user growth enough to offset cannibalization of legacy workflows. The market is moving from asking whether Adobe has AI to asking whether AI changes consolidated growth.

96. OIL + PPI + FED: Producer inflation is already transmitting the energy shock: August final-demand energy rose 4.2% and diesel jumped 24.1%, while Brent closed at $107.63. The key read-through is that the Fed is facing a supply-side inflation problem, not simply overheated demand. Hiking into an energy shock can suppress demand without creating more oil supply, which raises stagflation risk.

97. APPLE RELATIVE STRENGTH: Apple rose 3.6% while the S&P 500 fell 0.58% and Nvidia and Micron sold off. That divergence suggests investors temporarily treated the hardware product cycle as less duration-sensitive than AI infrastructure. The test is whether higher energy prices and borrowing costs eventually weaken consumers enough to overwhelm the product-cycle catalyst.

98. TRUCKING CAPITAL CYCLE: Bernstein turned constructive on XPO, Saia and Knight-Swift as trucking supply continues to reset. The non-consensus angle is supply: if weaker operators and drivers exit while fleet investment stays constrained, today's pressure can create tomorrow's pricing power. This is a classic capital-cycle setup where bad near-term economics can improve future industry structure.

99. LABCORP QUALITY OF GROWTH: Labcorp's 2029 framework pairs 5%-8% revenue growth with 8.5%-11.5% EPS growth and 75-150 bps of margin expansion. That spread implies the investment case depends on operating leverage and capital allocation, not just volume. If free cash flow grows in line with earnings as guided, buybacks and bolt-on M&A can become meaningful contributors to per-share compounding.

100. MARKET REGIME: The S&P 500 has fallen roughly 2% over four sessions while oil, bond yields and Fed-hike odds rise together. This is different from a conventional growth scare, where bonds usually rally as stocks fall. When stocks and long-duration bonds both struggle, near-term cash flow and pricing power become more valuable relative to distant-duration narratives.
